meta.title: J++ — A native code editor for the Mac
meta.description: J++ is a fast, native code editor for macOS. Edit in 95 languages, run and debug your code, query databases with SQL, work with GitHub and ask an AI assistant, with nothing extra to install.

hero.title: Everything around your code. Nothing in the way.
hero.text: J++ is a fast, native code editor for the Mac. Write in 95 languages, run and debug your code, query your data with SQL, push to GitHub and ask an AI assistant, all in one small app.
hero.app_store: Get it on the Mac App Store
hero.note: Free download · {size} · macOS 12 or later · Apple silicon and Intel
hero.image_alt: The J++ window: a file explorer on the left, tabs, and a Python file with syntax colouring.

why.title: What makes it different.
why.text: Most editors start empty and ask you to assemble the rest. J++ starts complete, and it is made for the Mac and nothing else.

items.title: Truly native
items.text: Built with Cocoa for macOS, not a web page inside a wrapper. It starts fast, behaves like the rest of your Mac, and the whole app is a download of less than 10 MB.

items.title: Complete from the first launch
items.text: Run, debug, IntelliSense, SQL, GitHub and AI are part of the app. There is no marketplace to search and no extensions to choose, set up and keep updated.

items.title: Your data is one query away
items.text: Run SQL on Databricks, Snowflake, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and SQLite. Even an Excel workbook or a CSV file becomes a table you can query.

items.title: AI on your terms
items.text: Connect your own Claude API key, any OpenAI-compatible service, or a model running on your Mac. J++ has no subscription, and your code is sent only when you ask.

items.title: Private by design
items.text: No account, no analytics, no advertising, no tracking. Passwords, tokens and API keys are kept in the macOS Keychain.

items.title: At home on your Mac
items.text: Liquid Glass on macOS 26, SF Symbols, SF Mono, and light and dark appearances that follow the system. One app for Apple silicon and Intel.

items.title: An editor that keeps up with you.
items.text: The editing engine is Scintilla, known for its speed with large files. Around it, J++ adds the tools you use all day.
bullets: Syntax colouring and code folding for 95 languages
Multiple cursors, column editing, macros and bookmarks
Find, replace and mark with regular expressions, across all open files
A file explorer that follows the folder as it changes
Session restore that keeps even your unsaved text
items.alt: The J++ editor with the explorer sidebar and a Python file.

items.title: It knows your code.
items.text: Completion as you type, parameter hints, descriptions when the pointer rests on a name, and marks under errors and warnings.
bullets: C, C++, Objective-C and Swift work at once, with the language servers that come with Xcode
Python works with no server at all: J++ reads your file and your installed modules
Go, Rust, TypeScript, Java, Ruby, Lua and more are used when their servers are on your Mac
items.alt: A completion list showing the members of a Python object.

items.title: Press F5. In any language.
items.text: Compile and Run work for every language in the menu. The output appears under your code, and after an error the caret jumps to the line the compiler names.
bullets: A Python debugger with breakpoints, stepping, the variables of the frame and an expression field
Built-in checks for JSON, XML, YAML, TOML, HTML, CSS and more
Manage Compilers shows what is installed and downloads what is missing with Homebrew, npm or pip
items.alt: The Python debugger paused on a line, with the variables listed beside the output.

items.title: SQL, right next to your code.
items.text: Save your connections once, then press ⌘↩ in a SQL tab. The results arrive in a grid you can copy or export as CSV.
bullets: Databricks and Snowflake through their own SQL APIs
PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Azure SQL
SQLite files, with nothing to install
Excel workbooks and CSV files: every sheet becomes a table
items.alt: A SQL query over an Excel workbook, with the results in a grid under the code.

items.title: An assistant that sees what you see.
items.text: Ask a question and the assistant reads the file in front of you and your selection. Insert and Replace Selection put the answer's code into the editor as one undo step.
bullets: Ready-made questions: Explain Code, Find Problems, Improve Code, Add Comments, Write Tests
Claude models with your own API key, with answers that appear as they are written
Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including a local model such as Ollama
items.alt: The assistant panel beside the editor, explaining a bug in the selected function.

items.title: From clone to push, without leaving.
items.text: Connect your account and J++ lists your repositories. The status bar shows the branch, what there is to push or pull, and how many files changed.
bullets: Clone, commit, push, pull and fetch
Publish a folder to a new repository
Create a gist from a file, or copy a link to the current line
items.alt: The Clone Repository window with the list of the account's repositories.

less.title: What you will not find in J++.

items.title: No extensions
items.text: Everything on this page is in the app the first time you open it.

items.title: No account
items.text: You never sign in to J++. There is nothing to create.

items.title: No subscription
items.text: The AI assistant uses your own key or your own local model.

items.title: No telemetry
items.text: J++ does not measure you, and sends nothing to its author.

guide.text: Help ▸ J++ Guide describes each feature step by step, with screenshots in light and dark, and a table of every keyboard shortcut.

privacy_page.title: Privacy Policy
privacy_page.description: J++ does not collect any data about you.
privacy_page.intro: J++ is a code editor for the Mac made by Jason Leiton. It does not collect any data about you.

sections.title: What J++ does not do
sections.body: J++ has no accounts, no analytics, no advertising and no tracking. It does not send your files, your code, or any information about how you use the app to the developer or to anyone else.

sections.title: Your files
sections.body: J++ opens only the files and folders you choose. They stay on your Mac. To reopen your previous session, J++ keeps a list of those files, and a copy of unsaved text, in its own private folder on your Mac.

sections.title: Services you connect
sections.body:
J++ talks to other services only when you set them up and ask for something:

  • Databases. If you add a database connection, your queries go directly from your Mac to the server you entered.
  • GitHub. If you connect a GitHub account, J++ uses it to list your repositories, to clone, push and pull, and to create gists when you ask.
  • AI models. If you connect a model, the question you type, and the file and selection you chose to include, are sent to that model's provider (for example Anthropic) when you press Send. That provider's own terms and privacy policy apply to what it receives.

Connection details are stored on your Mac, and passwords, tokens and API keys are stored in the macOS Keychain. None of this passes through the developer of J++.

sections.title: This website
sections.body: This website uses no cookies, no analytics and no third-party scripts. The language you pick with the EN | ES switch is remembered in your own browser and is not sent anywhere.

sections.title: Changes
sections.body: If this policy changes, the new version will be published on this page with a new date.

support_page.title: Support
support_page.description: Answers to the most common questions about J++.
support_page.intro: This page answers the most common questions. The full guide is inside the app: choose Help ▸ J++ Guide.

sections.title: Installing J++
sections.body:
Open the downloaded disk image and drag J++ to your Applications folder. J++ needs macOS 12 or later and runs on Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

If macOS says it cannot check the app the first time you open it, open System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security, find the message about J++ and press Open Anyway.

sections.title: Compile or Run says a tool comes with Xcode
sections.body: J++ uses Apple's developer tools for C, C++, Objective-C, Swift, Python and Git. Install Xcode from the App Store, or run xcode-select --install in Terminal, then try again.

sections.title: A language has no compiler yet
sections.body: Choose Run ▸ Manage Compilers…. The list shows which compilers are installed; tick the missing ones and press Install Selected to download them with Homebrew, npm or pip.

sections.title: Running SQL
sections.body: Open Database ▸ Manage Connections… (⇧⌘D), add a connection, then press ⌘↩ in a SQL tab. Results appear under your code. PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server need their command line clients, which you can install with Homebrew.

sections.title: Debugging Python
sections.body: Click the margin next to a line to set a breakpoint, then press F6. Use the toolbar to step through the code.

sections.title: The Mac App Store version
sections.body: Apple requires App Store apps to run in a sandbox, so that version uses only the tools from macOS and Xcode. It cannot start a program it has just built from C, C++ or Objective-C, and it does not offer PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server connections. When a compiler needs other files in the same folder, press Allow Folder Access… in the output pane.

sections.title: Contact
sections.body: Write to {email}. Please include your macOS version and what you were doing.
